speechtext: Questions and comments are now terminated. The Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Keeper) on debate.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the one thing that we can say with some confidence about this Budget is that it is clearly unfair to ordinary Canadians. It is a kick in the teeth of the ordinary taxpayers. The real question that must be asked about the Budget is who pays the bill that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) presented with his Budget in the House. It is obviously the ordinary taxpayer of the country who will pay. Every ordinary family across the country will be paying an increase in taxes of approximately $500 a year. That is one heck of a wallop in terms of increased taxes. That increase in taxes comes on top of the $500 increase in taxes of ordinary Canadians by the Minister of Finance last November 8. That is unfair, Mr. Speaker, because at the same time as he is asking ordinary Canadians to pay increased taxes, he is telling other Canadians that they can rest in the sunshine of paying no taxes.
As a result of the Budget, the Government will have collected $4.1 billion in personal income taxes by 1990-91. As a result of the Budget, the Government will be collecting $2.6 billion more in sales tax by the year 1990. At the same time, corporate taxes are going down and by 1990-91, they will be $2.2 billion less. This obviously makes the Budget very unfair and unbalanced. Ordinary families will pay $500 more in taxes while corporations will benefit next year by some $540 million less taxes. They will pay even less in corporate taxes as years progress.
The Budget-Mr. Keeper
When the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) announced the Western Accord in the House, she was very proud to say that consumers would not have to carry the burden as a result of that energy accord. Of course, the day she announced that accord there was no mention of a tax for consumers, only the fact that the oil companies were getting a $2 billion tax holiday.
We waited some time for the other shoe to drop. When the Minister of Finance delivered his Budget, we discovered that the gift to the oil companies as a result of the Western Accord will come out of the pockets of consumers. The Minister of Finance raised the excise tax on gasoline by two cents a litre.
From a political perspective, the Budget was well crafted because the impact of tax increases on individuals are delayed and spread out among several groups. For instance, the gasoline tax increase will not take effect for a few months so that consumers will not feel its immediate impact. However, the truth remains that the Government has raised taxes on gasoline in order to pay for that tax holiday to the oil companies.
The measure which received the greatest applause from the Conservative caucus during the Budget presentation was the capital gains tax exemption of $500,000 over a lifetime. While I support a capital gains tax exemption for such things as the sale of family farms and individual homes, allowing $500,000 in capital gains tax exemption while increasing the taxes for ordinary Canadians is completely unacceptable. At a time when the Government is preaching restraint, it is unfair to allow capital gains tax exemptions to a select few. The Government is raising sales taxes and limiting indexation on personal income tax while allowing a capital gains tax exemption to those who have money. The most outstanding feature of the Budget is its unfairness. It favours corporations and the rich. [Translation]
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, this Budget is unfair, for it has raised taxes paid by ordinary people while at the same time reducing those paid by rich people and large corporations. [English]
I hear comments about the coalition. I presume it is envy that this Party has been able to bring progress and a breath of fresh air to politics in Ontario.
Let me comment on the capital gains tax from the perspective of its use as an economic instrument. It perhaps would be possible to understand the Government's decision to tax middle income earners while favouring the rich if the capital gains exemption were to achieve a worth-while public purpose.
In the opinion of the Minister of Finance, the capital gains tax exemption would create employment and result in economic growth. I suggest that opinion deserves further study. First, the Minister has set no conditions for the capital gains tax exemption. For instance, he did not make this exemption conditional on creating employment in our country where there are 1.5 million people unemployed. He did not say that if you invest in Canada you can have this exemption on capital gains, which would be a worth-while public purpose. He just

May 29, 1985
The Budget-Mr. Keeper
said, "You can have a tax holiday on capital gains whatever you do."
It is important for us to take note that even before this Budget, capital gains was treated much more favourably than ordinary income. Up until the Budget, half of one's capital gains would be tax free anyway. What the Minister has done is sweeten the pot, and the pot was already pretty sweet as it was.
What was the result of the previous easy treatment of capital gains by the tax system? Did it result in a great deal of new employment? Had the Minister examined the results of those capital gains, studied them and come up with documentation to demonstrate to us that this kind of use of the taxation system resulted in x number of jobs or that it directed employment into regionally underdeveloped areas? No, Mr. Speaker. The Government simply moved on the basis of blind faith, on the basis of philosophy and its ideological commitment to laissez-faire, to hands off, when it comes to the private sector.
Let us consider some other possibilities that capital gains might be used for. If you had a summer cottage and it was worth a tidy bit, you might want to sell it and realize a capital gain and a tax benefit therefrom. Would that create employment? Not necessarily. If you owned a duplex or a triplex, a building in which you did not live yourself, and you wanted to realize an exemption under capital gains so you sold the dwelling, would that result in more employment? No, not that I can see, Mr. Speaker. If you invested outside of the country, even if it created employment wherever you invested, would that make jobs for Canadians? It is pretty hard for me to see that it would. It is possible for somebody to sell a condo in Florida and realize a capital gain that will not be taxed, to get a gift from the Government, but it would not create any employment in Canada.
Another way capital gains will have an impact is that they are treated better under the taxation system than dividends or interest. It will favour trading in shares. Does that necessarily result in employment? Not necessarily, Mr. Speaker. What proportion of the economic activity that will take place under this exemption of capital gains will favour employment? I do not know. I am sure the Government does not know either. It did not provide us with any figures. If the Government did know, it would have provided us with solid figures to say that this tax holiday will provide 1,000 or 10,000 new jobs. The Government provided no figures because the Government does not know how many jobs will be created as a result. The Government does not know how much of this money from the Government going to those who have large capital holdings will be a waste because there will be no employment creation whatsoever.
When we are looking at this capital gains tax holiday, we are talking about a fair amount of money. It is not a minor item. This year we are talking about some $550 million. That is a lot of money which the Government is giving up, particularly at a time when it says that it is concerned about balancing the books and reducing the deficit.
Next year we will lose from public revenues some $700 million. In five years, when this capital gains exemption reaches its full proportions, you will be looking at billions of dollars, Mr. Speaker. It is a serious question. You have to ask yourself, why did the Government introduce this capital gains holiday? It could not have been because the Government was concerned about reducing the deficit. If the Government were, it would have sought to collect this revenue and to use it to bring down the deficit.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, I have another comment to make on the question of capital gains. It is important to me that the public be the real winner every time tax exemptions are granted, and the first and foremost consideration today is unemployment and jobs. Does the Government know how many new jobs will flow from this measure? I would suggest that no one not even the Government, can come up with exact figures.
Mr. Speaker, I want to know why they gave that tax exemption to rich people without any guarantee that it will create jobs in Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Thank you, I just keep trying.

I see, Sir, that I have only two minutes remaining. I want to be sure to mention one other item from the Budget because it is crucial. The most shocking element of this Budget is the meat axe which the Government took to the pension system. It decided to limit indexation of the old age pension. The Government is taking away from the people who built this country their sense of security. The Government has decided that the first 3 per cent of inflation will not be covered in pensions. This year I think pensioners will lose $100, and next year the amount will be more. The social policy reform group has estimated the cumulative loss to a single pensioner by the year 1987, two years from now, will be $1,577.
This Government has decided to pick the pockets of pensioners in order to give money to its friends in business to whom the Government is giving a tax holiday. That is the most cruel, insensitive aspect of this Budget. The Government has broken promises. It said universality was a sacred trust and that it would govern with compassion. Who did the government hit over the head?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The elderly.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, the elderly. The Government is taking money out of the pockets of elderly Canadians to give a capital gains holiday to its friends, a move which is of questionable benefit in terms of employment or of any economic impact.
It is shocking that the Government would tamper with the pensions of people who have built this country when the
May 29, 1985

Government promised during the election that universality and pensions were sacred.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gerry Weiner (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to salute a new day for Canada. My colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), has shown us the way to economic renewal. He has opened the door of success to Canadians. He has given us the chance to rebuild Canada. The future is ours.
For over a decade the door to success was kept closed, barred by a massive debt and the economic policies of the previous administration, policies which never recognized the great potential within every individual Canadian. Instead, we saw policies which shattered the morale of Canadians, that lead to stagnation in the economy and destroyed the dreams of millions of Canadians. A shattered dream is hard to repair; a shattered notion, even harder.
We have begun the process of repair and renewal, a process which will give new hopes to Canadians, a process which offers all Canadians a chance to grow, a chance to succeed. The Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner), when he was Minister of Finance, showed us the way to go into debt. Canadians accepted it then; after all, it was not that much and they were told that it was necessary and unavoidable. However, it set a dangerous trend, a trend of always taking the easy way out, a trend which led to more and more debt, and a trend which has led to a deficit of some $35 billion this year alone.
Tough measures were needed a long time ago, but the previous administration was afraid to act. In 1975, one in eight tax dollars was used to pay the interest on our debt. The previous administration had set sail on a course which lead the country further and further into debt, with more and more misery for thousands of Canadians. It lead us to a point where 30 per cent of our tax dollars go to pay only the interest on the debt. When Members of the previous administration spoke to Canadians, they never told them that 80 per cent of the income tax they paid would one day go to paying the interest on the debt.
We have taken tough measures. They are fair and they are progressive. They are positive steps toward a new future for Canadians. I can understand the Opposition's mock rage, its posturing in the House, because the Budget shows Canadians that we are willing and able to make changes, fair changes which will provide more jobs and offer them new hope, something the previous administration was unable to do. Instead, it took us into debt and shattered our dreams. On September 4, Canadians voted for a change. They voted for a chance at a new beginning.
This Government has chosen a path which brings about positive, fair change. The Minister of Finance has adopted a fair approach which will solve the problem over time without threatening our economic recovery. This is not an easy task. We cannot ask Canadians to do it by themselves. Government must be a leader in cutting costs and eliminating waste. Eighty
The Budget-Mr. Weiner
per cent of our actions to reduce the deficit will result from our efforts to cut government expenditures.

Very important though they were, these measures would not have been enough and some taxes had to be increased. As a whole, however, these increases will amount to only $250 million in 1985-86 and $1.7 billion in 1986-87. In other words, close to 80 per cent of the deficit reduction stems from lower expenditures. It is a fair and realistic strategy under the present circumstances with the result that, within a relatively short time, the Government will have more leeway to take yet more encouraging measures for Canadians.

Our goal is growth and new jobs. During the election we spoke of jobs, jobs, jobs. That is still our goal. Unlike the opposition Parties that are still wandering around in the dark, the Minister of Finance has lit a beacon of hope, a beacon which will guide Canada through the shoals of Liberal mismanagement to a new economic future.
This Budget will generate new economic activity and with that activity will come new jobs. The small business sector has long been proven to be the major source of new jobs in this country. In my own riding of Dollard, small business was stagnating, its spirit crushed by the ineptitude of the previous administration. It has been awaiting some sign that the Government cares, that the Government recognizes its ability to create jobs, permanent jobs. I was a small-businessman, and I beleive that small business is the single most dynamic force in the Canadian economy. More jobs, permanent jobs, have been created by this sector than by any other. The last Liberal Government with its spending on mammoth projects, work schemes, et cetera, which quickly became modern day dinosaurs, was not the answer. Past policies made it easier to keep wealth than to create it. These savings vehicles did not create jobs, they left investment decisions in the hands of bankers and their best customer has been the Canadian Government. I hope I need not remind too many people of issues like Dome and Maislin. I am not an economist, but I know that what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), the Minister of Finance and we in the Government have done in the Budget has broken with the past and has taken a gamble, a gamble on the Canadian people. A number of elements in the Budget will make it easier for the average Canadian on the street to say: "I would be better off investiong in a small business than just putting my money to sleep in a savings account."
In my riding, 61 per cent of Challenge '85 applications came from small-businessmen whose morale was on the way up, who say this Government take the first progressive steps in November and who wanted to show Canadians that our faith in them as the vehicle of economic renewal was not unfounded. We want to encourage Canadians to invest in Canada's growth. By giving Canadians a lifetime capital gains exemption of $500,000, the Government is giving individual Canadians a chance to invest in Canada's future. Unlike the NDP, we know that most investors are ordinary Canadians, not multi-millionaires.

May 29, 1985
The Budget-Mr. Weiner
We are rewarding success and challenging Canadians to invest in Canadian enterprise. We believe they will accept the challenge.
We have also for the first time changed the regulations governing RRSP and pension fund investment. RRSP funds can be used for investment in smaller Canadian businesses. Does the Opposition actually think this opportunity will be ignored? No, it will not. There will be a new influx of badly needed capital for business. This is but one important step which will create jobs. We have made other changes to pensions that will benefit all Canadians. Portability of pensions is now a reality. No longer will it be necessary for a Canadian to turn down a job offer or refuse a new opportunity because his pension is frozen.
Men and women are equal. They deserve equal pay for equal work, and they deserve equal pensions. The Government has recognized that equality and has acted.
As I mentioned before, we must be fair. The Budget recognized the fact that our social programs must help those in need. That is where the money must be channelled. We have kept universality but for the first time the Government is insisting that the moneys go to those who need it. We have increased the child tax credit, a credit delivered to low income families, to a level of $584 per child by 1989, an increase of $140. At the same time we have guaranteed that Old Age Security payments or family allowances will not be reduced as a result of the modification to indexation. They will be fully compensated whenever inflation goes over 3 per cent. The Guaranteed Income Supplement, as well as benefits paid to veterans, will continue to be fully indexed.
When one considers fairness, we cannot forget taxing the rich. All Canadians should be making a reasonable contribution to the tax revenues required to finance public sector operations which benefit all. This Budget recognizes that principle. Beginning in 1986 there will be a minimum tax. High income Canadians will pay their share. Unlike the infamous MacEachen Budget, which introduced 35 retroactive taxes, we believe in being fair and honest with the Canadian people. We have no retroactive taxes, and we are giving advance notice of when we intend to make changes. That is the fair way, the progressive way.
We recognize the role labour has to play in creating jobs. We have seen in Quebec the successful application of labour-sponsored venture capital funds. With the progressive use of tax credits to individuals investing in these funds, we will increase investment in small and medium sized businesses. This will create jobs.
Research and development in Canada has long been ignored. We recognize the vital contribution it can make to Canada's economic growth. We have made changes that will help these smaller companies, especially start-up firms. This Government will make 100 per cent of the tax credit they now earn for R and D refundable to them. This is a major,
significant improvement over the 40 per cent of the credit that was previously refundable.
This sector was ignored by the previous administration. Its full job creating potential was never recognized, and its need for capital never realized. The Government has recognized the potential this sector holds for Canada. We have recognized its needs. If Canadian industry is to be successful in the 21st century, it must rely on research and development today. We recognize that and we have acted. Not only will we create jobs today, we have guaranteed them in the years ahead. We face a great challenge. Our challenge is to recreate a dynamic Canada, one of growth and prosperity.
Last Friday, in Paris, Yves Duhaime, Quebec's new finance minister, was asked what he thought of the P.C. Budget. Does anyone remember what he said? He stood up and declared loud and clear that it is about time somebody in Ottawa took a stand and said, "Enough is enough." What he meant, and what we mean, is that the federal Government cannot continue to support the country as if it were receiving welfare. It is about time the people of Canada did this for themselves. That is what my Party believes in. This is what the Minister of Finance's Budget is designed to achieve. It is intended to arouse the people of Canada so that they can improve the deplorable economic situation in this country through hard work, investment in Canadian business and intelligent risk taking. No Government in the world can tolerate an annual deficit as large as ours in relation to our country's size. The Liberals tried it and look where they are now. They deserve it.
When the Liberals came to power-there was no deficit. There was a surplus. Through their financial incompetence, the term "deficit" has become, unfortunately, a household word in Canada.
[ Translation]
In 1974-75 the federal Government's net debt was 16.6 per cent of the Gross National Product. In 1984-85 it has reached 45.2 per cent-a totally unacceptable level.
The measures proposed in this Budget will directly reduce the deficit. That is precisely what Canadians expected us to do, and we will manage to reduce our deficit so that our children may look to the future with confidence.

During the election campaign we promised to act responsibly. Our Budget is the first step in that direction. I will tell Hon. Members something-it is about time! Through our Budget, every small and medium sized businessman in Canada is being invited and encouraged to invest with confidence in the economic future of Canada. This is what will provide jobs for Canadians. We have provided a way for the Canadian people to help themselves.
[ Translation]
The budgetary proposals manage to reduce the deficit while introducing measures to help create durable jobs. To create those jobs, Canada needs a private sector that is dynamic and vigorous, flexible and innovative. Small- and medium-sized
May 29, 1985

businesses in particular are the engine of our economy. By encouraging the private initiative of Canadians with measures such as the lifetime capital gains exemption of half a million dollars and allowing pension funds and registered retirement savings plans to invest in small businesses, we will create employment and provide for sustained economic growth.
Many jobs will also be created as a result of measures to promote investment in research and development.

Before our sweep of September 4, media commentators and other political observers were deploring the fact that there was little difference between the Liberal and Conservative platforms. The Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent) compared the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Leader of the Opposition to Visa and Mastercard respectively. He implied the voters had no choice. However, the massive shift of allegiance has shown that the voters themselves saw the significant differences between our two Parties.
Our gains were most spectacular in Quebec. However, right across the country, French-speaking people and members of many ethnic communities joined their English-speaking brethren in deserting the Liberal Party. They rejected bureaucracy. They rejected federal paternalism and the period of confrontation. We must eliminate waste and inefficiency in Government. We want a Government which is efficient, effective and economical. Stop betting on the Government, and bet on the little guy.
Where was the Government in February of 1984 when the petrochemical industry of Montreal called? At that time, there was no response. What did the Government do with respect to the losses in Montreal's pharmaceutical industry? We waited some 15 years for a review of a patent law which was totally unfair. It was a law which cost us jobs and proved disastrous to the development of products.
This Budget is a call to arms to our constituency-the small businessman, the professionals and the farmers-all 700,000 of us. We form a veritable army in the war on unemployment. It is this army which will create jobs. This Budget is a break from the past. We want to use the creative energy of Canadians to build a better future for themselves.
What did September 4 signify? It signified a change of Government, yes. However, it also signified the beginning of a new political area. In November, we promised to put our House in order. This means a leaner Government, one which is more efficient-one which will create a healthier investment climate. We have said that Canada is open for business.
The Budget embodies three main principles of the P.C. Government: the encouragement of private initiative and job creation; the improvement of the management and effectiveness of government; and concrete action to control the debts.
Measures to encourage private initiative represent a break with the past. Personal capital gains exemptions are designed
The Budget-Mr. Weiner
to let the people of Canada-not politicians and bureaucrats- choose where to invest and how to create jobs. What the Budget says to individuals and communities is, "For too long Government has made your decisions for you." Now is the time to translate ideas and energies into the type of Canada we want for ourselves and our children.
Canadians are not quitters, Mr. Speaker. We are tough and resilient. Together, we can work toward a greater future-a future with a job, success and where the security of one's family is guaranteed.
Some Hon. Members; Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, 1 have a comment to make.
This Budget is not a beacon of light, as outlined by the previous speaker. It is a revisiting of the Dark Ages. The Conservative philosophy is nothing more than economic Nean-derthalism, which is no more apparent than in this Budget.
For one group in the economy, that is, people in communities dependent upon the fishing industry, the Budget is a complete disaster. For this group, the Conservative Party has broken all its promises. Instead of assisting these people with measures such as salmon enhancement programs, fishing vessel buy-back programs, more work on habitat protection, and the development of an effective fishing industry plan, the Conservative Government has cut the Department of Fisheries and Oceans' Budget by $65 million. It has increased user fees. It has increased mortgage rates and cut services to the industry. This Budget is not fair. It is not effective for the fishing industry and in fact it is irrational.
